--- title: "[Graph.cmty_stochastic_block_model()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Fit a stochastic block model to this graph using expectation-maximization. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L31185-L31412){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.cmty_stochastic_block_model( k=2, max_iter=100, tol=1e-06, seed=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Stochastic block model](/assets/graphs/cmty-stochastic-block-model.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two dense clusters, a triangle A, B, C and a four-node cluster D, E, F, G, joined by the single edge C to D. A two-block model fitted with seed 7 puts each cluster in its own block, dense inside and sparse between, drawn in the accent color and teal. The card lists block 0 as D, E, F, G and block 1 as A, B, C." width="100%"} Partitions nodes into `k` blocks by alternately estimating the block interaction matrix and reassigning each node to its most probable block, until the assignments settle. A stochastic block model (SBM) assumes that every node belongs to one of `k` blocks and that the chance of an edge between two nodes depends only on their blocks. Fitting the model means finding the block assignment (and the matrix of block-to-block edge probabilities) that best explains the observed edges. Each iteration has two steps: - estimate the edge probability between every pair of blocks from the current assignments (edges present divided by node pairs possible) - move every node to the block under which its pattern of edges and non-edges is most likely, given the current assignments of all other nodes This is a "hard" EM variant: each node is given a single block rather than a probability over blocks. Unlike modularity-based methods, an SBM is not limited to finding dense clusters, so it is useful for: - community detection when you know (or want to fix) the number of groups - finding core-periphery or bipartite-like structure, where nodes are grouped by *how* they connect rather than by being densely connected to each other - producing a compact, generative summary of a network's large-scale structure Caveats: the fit starts from a random assignment and can get stuck in a poor local optimum, including putting every node in a single block, so results vary with `seed=`; it is worth trying several seeds and comparing. Some blocks may end up empty, so fewer than `k` distinct block IDs can appear. Each iteration examines every pair of nodes for every block, which costs roughly `O(k * n^2)` time in pure Python, so this method is suited to graphs with at most a few thousand nodes. Edge weights are ignored. The model treats edges as undirected; on a directed graph only outgoing edges are counted and the within-block probabilities use undirected pair counts, so results there are approximate. The block assignments are always written to the node DataFrame, even when `return_dict=True`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of blocks (communities) to fit. Default is `2`. Must be at least `1`; `k=1` trivially places every node in block `0`. Larger values allow finer structure but make poor local optima more likely and increase the running time proportionally. [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of EM iterations. Default is `100`. Fitting usually stops earlier, once the convergence test on `tol=` succeeds; this is a safety cap for graphs where assignments keep oscillating. [tol]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1e-06]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Convergence tolerance on the log-likelihood change. Default is `1e-6`. Iteration stops once the total log-likelihood of the best assignments changes by less than this amount between consecutive iterations. Larger values stop earlier. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for the initial random block assignment. If `None` (default), a different initialization is used on every call, so results can differ between runs. Pass an integer for reproducible results. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute (node DataFrame column) to store assignments in. If `None` (default), uses `"sbm_block"`. Overwrites the column if it already exists. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a `{node_id: block_id}` dict instead of self. If `False` (default), stores the assignments in the node DataFrame and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping node IDs to block IDs (integers from `0` to `k - 1`; block numbers are arbitrary labels). An empty graph gives `{}`. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two dense groups, a triangle and a four-node clique, are joined by a single edge. A two-block model fitted with `seed=7` recovers the two groups as separate blocks: ::: {#1bf5a38a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]) graph.add_edges([ ("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), # triangle ("C", "D"), # bridge ("D", "E"), ("D", "F"), ("D", "G"), # four-node clique ("E", "F"), ("E", "G"), ("F", "G"), ]) blocks = graph.cmty_stochastic_block_model(k=2, seed=7, return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): block for nid, block in blocks.items()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'G': 0, 'C': 1, 'A': 1, 'E': 0, 'F': 0, 'D': 0, 'B': 1} ``` ::: ::: The fit depends on the random starting point. With `seed=42` the same graph converges to a single block, which is why it pays to try several seeds: ::: {#3d18d7c3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} blocks = graph.cmty_stochastic_block_model(k=2, seed=42, return_dict=True) set(blocks.values()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {0} ``` ::: ::: Without `return_dict=`, the assignments are stored in the node DataFrame (here under a custom column name) and the graph is returned for chaining: ::: {#7989bb4d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( graph .cmty_stochastic_block_model(k=2, seed=7, attr_name="block") .get_node_df() .select("label", "block") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
